newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal pay deal threatens inflation goal - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Portugal pay deal threatens inflation goal - analyst.

text.p: The three percent wage rise agreed with one public sector union will complicate the government's bid to cut inflation to 2.25-2.5 percent next year, analysts said on Wednesday.
"I believe that 2.5 percent is possible, but that seems to me the lowest possible level that could be achieved with this wage accord," said economist Isabel Cabral of brokers Fincor.
But a slight overshoot on the inflation target should not seriously endanger Portugal's chances of meeting the criteria for entry to the European Union's planned single currency, analysts add.

Making the grade for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) when it is launched in 1999 is Prime Minister Antonio Guterres' top policy priority, and the government used inflation as its main argument in the negotiations that ended with partial success on Tuesday.

The Maastricht Treaty blueprint for EMU says a candidate's inflation rate must be no more than 150 basis points above that of the best three members. Analysts put the cut-off rate at around three percent.

The wage accord, signed on Tuesday night with just one of three union groups representing the 500,000 public sector employees, also threatens the government's target of cutting the budget deficit to 2.9 percent of gross domestic product (GDP), analysts say.
The two other union groups, the Communist-led Common Front and the Union of State Technical Staff, linked to the opposition Social Democrats, both rejected the wage deal.
The two unions will consult members about future action. But the wage rise will be paid to all public sector employess, regardless of union affiliation.
Analysts said the wage deal would block any big fall in the prices of non-tradeable goods as wages make up a significant part of the index.
They calculate the full value of the wage accord at around 3.4 percent including fringe benefits.
Average inflation, the 12-month rolling figure that the government takes for its target, eased to 3.1 percent in November from 3.2 percent in October.
But prices of non-tradeable goods rose 4.9 percent year-on-year against 4.2 percent in October.

"To get to the 2.25 percent (the bottom of the government's range), it would have been necessary for non-tradeable price inflation to have slowed to around three percent (next year)," said one analyst at a Lisbon bank.
"But with this accord, that is practically impossible."
Public sector wages set the pace for the private sector, so rises there will probably be around 1.5 percentage points above the government's inflation goal, analysts said.

"It is likely that the (private sector) wage rises will be around 1.5 percent above expected inflation, possibly creating problems for the non-tradeable index which is what most worries the Bank of Portugal and the financial markets," said analyst Armindo Escalda of Banco Santander de Negocios Portugal.
